title: Letko Brosseau urges Advantage shareholders to vote against proposed $2.5-billion takeover
html:
An Advantage Energy facility in Saddle Hills County, Alta. Canadian Natural Resources has offered to acquire the natural-gas producer for $2.5-billion.David Hills/Supplied

A significant investor in Calgary-based natural-gas producer Advantage Energy Ltd. AAV-T is urging fellow shareholders to reject a $2.5-billion takeover offer from Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. CNQ-T, suggesting the bid is opportunistic and undervalues the company.

Montreal-based investment manager Letko, Brosseau & Associates Inc. said in a Friday news release that it intends to vote against the proposed deal. Letko Brosseau controls about 5.5 per cent of Advantage’s shares, and is an established institutional fund manager with $23.4-billion in assets.

Canadian Natural announced an agreement on Nov. 16 to buy Advantage, its smaller rival, for $13.55 per share in cash. That was a 25-per-cent premium to Advantage’s average share price over the previous 30 trading days and valued the company at $2.53-billion, including debt.

The deal is part of a recent wave of consolidation driven by renewed investor interest in Canada’s oil and gas sector, as larger producers snap up smaller rivals.

But Letko Brosseau contends that Advantage is on solid financial footing and should feel no pressure to pursue a deal when natural gas prices have been depressed and companies’ appetite for mergers is heating up.

The investment manager said Advantage can afford to be patient after it struck a separate deal in August to sell its assets in the Wembley area of Alberta for $316-million, alleviating near-term financial pressures.

“This is not a company that finds itself in dire financial straits, it’s not a company with poor assets. It’s not a company that in any way, shape or form needs to seek out a deal at the moment,” Letko Brosseau partner Alex Letko said in an interview.

Advantage declined to comment on Friday. The company said in a November news release that the deal with Canadian Natural was the outcome of “a comprehensive review of strategic alternatives,” overseen by a special committee of its board of directors.

The board unanimously approved the transaction and recommended that shareholders vote for it.

Canadian Natural did not respond to a request for comment.

By contrast, Letko Brosseau said Canadian Natural is seizing on “highly opportunistic timing designed to acquire premier, long-life assets at the bottom of the natural gas cycle and during a period of leadership transition.”

Advantage’s board is “weakly playing what is in reality a very good hand,” the investment manager said in its Friday release.

Advantage has been searching for a new chief executive officer since Michael Belenkie stepped down in June under pressure from activist investors. Board chair John Festival is serving as interim CEO.

Installing a new leader with a strategic plan for Advantage could “further unlock value for existing shareholders,” Letko Brosseau said. “Selling the company now abandons that potential.”

Letko Brosseau also suggested that Canadian Natural’s offer price amounts to just 0.8 times the value of Advantage’s proven and likely gas reserves. A competitor, Logan Energy Corp., received roughly double that valuation on its assets in a recent deal in the same Montney Formation region.

“That valuation gap, in our opinion, should not exist,” Mr. Letko said. “These are assets that are in high demand and that acquirers are willing to pay for.”

Public filings suggest that there are at least two large shareholders whose support would be vital in influencing the outcome of a vote to approve the transaction, which is expected to take place in January 2027.

Toronto-based companies EdgePoint Investment Group Inc. and Mackenzie Financial Corp. respectively own 11.3-per-cent and 10.5-per-cent stakes in Advantage, according to data from FactSet.

An activist investor that was pushing for changes at Advantage, Kimmeridge Energy Management Co., reportedly held a 7-per-cent stake when the deal was announced, and has signalled its support, calling the deal “an excellent outcome for shareholders,” according to Bloomberg News.

Letko Brosseau’s opposition is “a reflection of our own views,” based on the company’s research, Mr. Letko said.

“We’re just trying to use our voice to stand up for our clients and for shareholders.”

Editor’s note: An earlier version of this story cited Bloomberg data about the largest shareholders in Advantage Energy. Based on new information from Advantage Energy, the story has been updated to cite ownership data from FactSet.
summary: Natural gas producer can afford to be patient amid growing appetite for mergers, investment firm says
